passages.original: sed quomodo si in decem hominibus, quinque filiis, et quinque servis, pariter diceremus : horum decem, unus est dominus, et unus est pater : non utique omnium patrem, nec dominum omnium vocaremus : sic et in eo quod ait : Unus Deus et Pater omnium, aliorum Pater, aliorum Deus accipiendum est. Tale quid de creaturis, et de Deo etiam Zeno cum suis Stoicis suspicatur. Quem secutus Virgilius ait (AEneid. VI) : et :
passages.english: But just as, if among ten men, five sons and five slaves, we were to say equally, "Of these ten, one is the master and one is the father," we would certainly not call him father of all, nor master of all, so too in what he says, "One God and Father of all," it must be understood as Father of some and God of others. Zeno too, with his Stoics, supposes something of this kind about created things and about God. Following him, Virgil says (Aeneid VI): and:
passages.notes: The passage ends with "and:" because the Virgil quotations from Aeneid VI (presumably the lines on the spirit that sustains the world) are missing from the text as given. The Latin is "Tale quid", and "Tale quid de creaturis, et de Deo" could also mean "something of this kind both about creatures and about God".
